item.title: deciax: Running a Decision Model on TPU with JAX and Pallas
item.author: junyi.h@comp.nus.edu.sg (Junyi Hou)

item.content:encoded:
Routing a support ticket, checking whether it asks for a refund, and scoring its urgency all call for structured decisions. A model can return choices and probabilities directly, without generating a textual answer token by token.

Laya is a Decision Model that handles choice, score, and yes/no questions in a single forward pass. I ported its inference path to JAX and built deciax to run these models on TPU, then optimized the computation with Pallas.

In this benchmark1, a single TPU v6e chip reached a single-question p50 of 2.18 ms for the English model and 1.55 ms for the multilingual model. The fastest measured results on A100 SXM4, H100 PCIe, and H200 NVL were 6.4 / 4.0 ms, 4.8 / 3.2 ms, and 5.8 / 4.1 ms, respectively (English / multilingual).

At 50 questions per call, v6e Pallas reached 33.69 / 17.83 ms, roughly 2.3× faster than plain JAX. The fastest measured A100, H100, and H200 results were 68.8 / 36.2 ms, 44.0 / 23.2 ms, and 39.8 / 21.2 ms, respectively.

# One input, several decisions

deciax takes an input and a set of questions, then returns structured results. Here is a duplicate-charge ticket:

import deciax

decider = deciax.load("laya")
result = decider.decide(
 {"user": "I was charged twice this month. Please refund the duplicate."},
 {
 "department": {
 "type": "choice",
 "instructions": "Which department should handle this?",
 "criteria": {
 "billing": "payments, invoices, refunds",
 "technical": "bugs, outages, system errors",
 "other": "everything else",
 },
 },
 "urgency": {
 "type": "score",
 "instructions": "How urgent is this?",
 "criteria": ["not urgent", "soon", "blocking"],
 },
 "refund_requested": {
 "type": "noul",
 "instructions": "Does the user ask for a refund?",
 },
 },
)
print(result)

# Move the inference path to JAX

deciax preserves Laya’s input construction, ModernBERT encoder, and decision heads while moving inference to JAX. Its runtime does not require PyTorch, Transformers, or Laya; the checkpoints and tokenizer still come from the original model. It also offers a /v1/systemone HTTP endpoint. The project documentation lists its current scope.

# Start with the baseline: PyTorch eager and JAX

Measurements ran on Oct 12, 2026, across RTX 3090, A100 SXM4, RTX A6000, H100 PCIe, and H200 NVL hosts, plus single-chip TPU v5e and v6e runs.

Latency figures show warmed in-process p50 per call2, including input encoding, inference, and result handling. Solid bars show p50; dashed markers show p95.

First, compare PyTorch eager on GPU with ordinary JAX on TPU:

For English single-question calls, GPU eager p50 ranged from 13.3 to 25.8 ms, while v6e JAX took 2.27 ms. At 50 questions, v6e JAX took 76.79 ms, compared with the lowest GPU eager result of 57.5 ms on H200 NVL. Multilingual followed a similar pattern: v6e JAX grew from 1.61 ms to 41.24 ms, while H200 eager took 34.0 ms at 50 questions.

# Where time goes: dispatch overhead and model computation

Next, break down baseline calls using the English model3:

Single-question GPU eager calls issue many small kernels: the English model used 1,090–1,213 cudaLaunchKernel calls per inference. The large remainder outside device execution points toward both kernel fusion and reducing dispatch overhead.

At 50 questions, computation accounts for most of the call. English v6e JAX took 76.79 ms end to end, with separately measured forward-only time of 71.27 ms and encoding near 3 ms. In XProf, dot_general and sub accounted for about 38% and 21% of this device time, directing attention to matrix computation and data movement in elementwise operations.

After the port, JAX operations serve as the baseline for exploring how to fuse computation on TPU. At the measured shapes, Pallas fuses multiple computations within each layer into one kernel4.

# Optimized: the fastest measured implementation on each platform

GPU testing covers TileLang, CUDA Graph, and torch.compile. We select the fastest measured implementation for each host, model, and question count to make the comparison as fair as possible. The TPU path uses v6e Pallas.

Single-question v6e Pallas p50 was 2.18 ms for English and 1.55 ms for multilingual. The lowest English GPU result was 4.8 ms on H100 PCIe using torch.compile with cudagraph; the lowest multilingual result was 3.2 ms. Pallas makes little difference relative to plain JAX at this shape.

At 50 questions, English v6e latency fell from 76.79 ms with JAX to 33.69 ms with Pallas; multilingual fell from 41.24 ms to 17.83 ms. These are speedups of 2.28× and 2.31×. English forward-only time fell from 71.27 ms to 28.25 ms, and multilingual from 36.54 ms to 13.36 ms.

# Latency as the question count grows

Connect the measurements at 1, 5, 10, and 50 questions to compare latency on H100, H200, and v6e Pallas:

# HTTP serving and installation

We also measured deciax.serve. For single-question calls over loopback with keep-alive, v6e Pallas HTTP p50 was 3.0 ms for English and 2.4 ms for multilingual. This includes the local HTTP round trip, but no external network latency or concurrent load test.

Use Python 3.14 or newer. Install it on a TPU host with:

python -m pip install "deciax[tpu]==0.1.1"

This release supports the Python interface example above. To inspect the Pallas implementation measured here, check out the corresponding code from the repository:

git clone https://github.com/Junyi-99/deciax.git
cd deciax
git checkout 6f3a930
uv sync --extra tpu

# Cost: Million model input tokens per US dollar

Cost compares only optimized English-model implementations: the fastest measured GPU variant and v6e Pallas on TPU. We calculate both on-demand and preemptible / spot scenarios.

Performance and price data were collected on Oct 12, 2026.

Prices are USD per GPU-hour or TPU chip-hour.

Hardware Provider On-demand Preemptible / Spot5
A100 SXM4 80GB Vast.ai $1.176 $0.727
H100 (SXM pricing) Nebius $4.500 $0.790
H200 (SXM pricing) Nebius $5.400 $0.790
TPU v6e Google Cloud $2.700 $0.970

The calculation is6:

Million model input tokens per US dollar
 = model input tokens per second × 3600 / hourly price / 1,000,000

Model input tokens include the ticket text repeated for each question.

# Conclusion

deciax brings Laya’s structured decisions to TPU. In this experiment, plain JAX already handled single-question calls in about 2 ms, with little additional benefit from Pallas at that shape. At 50 questions per call, the fused Pallas path was roughly 2.3× faster than plain JAX. The question count changes both the dominant overhead and the benefit of optimization.

For the inputs, models, and implementations tested here, v6e Pallas had lower latency than the compared GPU implementations at both one and 50 questions.

You can try deciax in Colab or explore the code in the GitHub repository.

  1. Performance data in this post comes from development commit 6f3a930. ↩︎

  2. Inputs use upstream’s Payout failing ticket with alternating noul and choice questions. Each series uses 20 warmups followed by 20 timed calls with device synchronization. ↩︎

  3. GPU p50 in the breakdown comes from the profiling companion timing series, separate from the preceding baseline figure. ↩︎

  4. The Pallas path in this report fuses normalization, QKV projection, RoPE, attention, output projection, and the MLP. For the path with sequence length at most 512, each layer uses one pallas_call. ↩︎

  5. Nebius Spot uses the starting price; TPU preemptible uses the report snapshot. ↩︎

  6. English calls contain 194 model input tokens at one question and 9,975 at 50 questions. We use the report’s recorded input tokens/s, derived from token counts divided by the original p50 latency. ↩︎

item.title: HLO Visualizer: Learn XLA HLO by Exploring It
item.author: junyi.h@comp.nus.edu.sg (Junyi Hou)
item.description: When working with JAX on TPU, you eventually need to read HLO. You want to know what a computation became after compilation, why extra copies appeared, or what is inside a fusion. The answers start with a compiler-generated text file. Instructions pack together shapes, layouts, tiling, memory spaces, and references to other computations. I built HLO Visualizer to make that easier. It turns HLO text into an explorable graph, with explanations of the instruction you select, piece by piece.
item.content:encoded:
When working with JAX on TPU, you eventually need to read HLO. You want to know what a computation became after compilation, why extra copies appeared, or what is inside a fusion. The answers start with a compiler-generated text file.

Instructions pack together shapes, layouts, tiling, memory spaces, and references to other computations.

I built HLO Visualizer to make that easier. It turns HLO text into an explorable graph, with explanations of the instruction you select, piece by piece.

# From seeing the graph to understanding an instruction

There is already an official HLO visualization tool: XProf’s Graph Viewer. It lets you explore an operation’s neighborhood, expand or collapse fusions, and connect the graph to profiling data. That is useful when you have identified an expensive operation and want to understand its dependencies. The official documentation describes this workflow.

HLO Visualizer puts the graph and the explanation in one interface. Nodes distinguish inputs, computation, transfers, and control flow. Select one to trace dependencies, inspect its original HLO, and navigate to the computations it references.

XProf connects HLO to measured performance. HLO Visualizer starts with a piece of HLO text you want to understand.

# Put the tutorial beside the instruction

Google DeepMind’s How to Scale Your Model has a useful introduction, How to read an XLA op. It explains names, types, layouts, memory locations, and operands through a fusion example. OpenXLA’s Operation semantics is the reference for precise operation behavior.

The next step is applying those rules to your own program.

Consider this simplified instruction:

%x = bf16[128,128]{1,0:T(8,128)(2,1)S(1)} parameter(0)

It contains several layers of information:

  • %x names the instruction’s result.
  • bf16[128,128] gives the logical type and shape.
  • 1,0 is the minor-to-major dimension order.
  • T(8,128)(2,1) describes two levels of physical tiling.
  • S(1) means VMEM in these TPU examples.
  • parameter(0) declares input 0 of the current computation.

The inspector breaks the original instruction into colored segments and explains its name, operation, operands, and attributes. Expand the type to inspect shape, dimension order, tiling, and memory space separately. Tuple elements can be explored individually too.

# Draw the TPU layout

Layout is an important part of HLO. Logical shape and physical storage layout describe different things. A 128 × 128 array can be split into tiles, with another level of tiling inside each tile. OpenXLA’s Shapes and layout and Tiled layout document the representation.

For the common TPU layout T(8,128)(2,1), HLO Visualizer draws a corner of a tile, labeling physical offsets and inner tile boundaries. The two sets of numbers become something you can see.

The tool also explains TPU memory locations such as HBM, VMEM, and SMEM, helping you interpret transfer instructions. Memory-space numbers depend on the backend; the explanations here use the project’s TPU v6e examples as their context.

# Start with a small program

The bundled examples come from 21 small JAX programs compiled on TPU v6e, each with HLO before and after optimization. Try attention for inputs and fusions, fori_matmul for loops, or gather_scatter for indexing operations.

Open an example, enter its entry computation from the sidebar, and select a node. Inspect its inputs and result type, then explore a computation referenced by a fusion or while. Switch between Before and After in Examples to inspect how compilation changes the graph.

To explore your own code, export HLO through JAX’s lowering and compilation interfaces:

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

def f(x, w):
 return jax.nn.relu(x @ w)

x = jnp.ones((128, 128), dtype=jnp.bfloat16)
w = jnp.ones((128, 128), dtype=jnp.bfloat16)
lowered = jax.jit(f).lower(x, w)

# HLO before optimization
print(lowered.as_text(dialect="hlo"))

# Compiled HLO; layouts and memory spaces depend on the backend
print(lowered.compile().as_text())

Copy either output and paste it through Open HLO. HLO text from XLA’s --xla_dump_to works too.

I want someone learning HLO for the first time to be able to connect the syntax to a small, real program. Open the graph, select an instruction, and follow the data.

Try HLO Visualizer. If it helps you understand your HLO, a star on GitHub is welcome. Please open an issue for instructions that are unclear or do not parse correctly.
